name: Choroidal folds
system: Special senses / Eye (choroid and retinal pigment epithelium)

clinicalPearls: Parallel grooves or striae involving the choroid, Bruch's membrane and retinal pigment epithelium, seen as alternating light and dark bands, usually horizontal, at the posterior pole

Arise from mechanical compression or shortening of the posterior wall of the eye; recognised causes include orbital mass lesions, thyroid eye disease, posterior scleritis, ocular hypotony, raised intracranial pressure with papilloedema, choroidal tumours and hyperopia
Idiopathic choroidal folds occur typically in hyperopic middle-aged men, are often bilateral and may be accompanied by disc oedema and a short axial length

On fluorescein angiography the crests appear hyperfluorescent, from stretched thinned RPE, and the troughs hypofluorescent, giving alternating bright and dark lines; OCT shows undulation of the RPE-Bruch's-choroid complex
New-onset unilateral folds, particularly with proptosis, a hyperopic shift or disc swelling, warrant orbital and neuro-imaging to exclude a retrobulbar mass or posterior scleritis
Inner retinal folds and choroidal folds may coexist or occur separately; distinguishing them helps localise the underlying cause
Management is directed at the underlying cause; longstanding idiopathic folds are usually stable and asymptomatic, although a hyperopic shift or mild distortion may occur
reference.pathophysiology: Choroidal folds arise when the outer coats of the eye, namely the sclera, choroid, Bruch's membrane and retinal pigment epithelium, are compressed, thickened or rendered redundant, throwing the choroid and overlying RPE into a series of parallel undulations. Any process that shortens or indents the posterior globe or expands the choroid may be responsible. Orbital masses and thyroid orbitopathy compress the globe, posterior scleritis inflames and thickens the sclera and choroid, hypotony allows the eye wall to collapse and fold, and raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath produces peripapillary folds with disc oedema. In idiopathic cases a short, thick sclera in a hyperopic eye is implicated. The crest of each fold has stretched, thinned RPE while the trough has heaped RPE, which produces the characteristic angiographic pattern.
additionalDifferentials: Inner retinal folds from an epiretinal membrane or hypotony
Angioid streaks (breaks in Bruch's membrane with a different, radiating pattern)
Orbital or choroidal tumour indenting the globe
Ocular hypotony following surgery, over-filtration or a wound leak
additionalInvestigations: OCT showing undulation of the RPE-Bruch's-choroid complex and any subretinal fluid
Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrating alternating hyper- and hypofluorescent bands
B-scan ultrasonography for posterior scleritis (T-sign), choroidal mass or scleral thickening
Orbital and brain imaging with CT or MRI where an orbital mass or raised intracranial pressure is suspected
Refraction to detect a hyperopic shift together with measurement of axial length
Measurement of intraocular pressure to identify hypotony, with thyroid function and orbital assessment where indicated
redFlags: New unilateral folds with proptosis or a hyperopic shift suggesting an orbital or retrobulbar mass
Pain, especially on eye movement, accompanying folds and suggesting posterior scleritis
Associated disc swelling raising the possibility of raised intracranial pressure
Hypotony with a shallow anterior chamber or a bleb leak after surgery
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic and longstanding choroidal folds are usually stable and visually insignificant. When secondary, the outcome depends on the underlying cause, and the folds may resolve if that cause, such as hypotony, an orbital mass or scleritis, is treated, although longstanding RPE changes can persist.
pitfalls: Dismissing new choroidal folds as idiopathic without imaging to exclude an orbital mass or posterior scleritis
Confusing choroidal folds with angioid streaks
Missing hypotony as a cause after glaucoma surgery or trauma
Overlooking associated papilloedema and raised intracranial pressure
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cause, since the folds themselves need no specific therapy — orbital decompression or tumour treatment for thyroid eye disease and orbital masses, corticosteroid immunosuppression for posterior scleritis, and correction of ocular hypotony
Lower raised intracranial pressure where papilloedema is responsible, through weight reduction, carbonic anhydrase inhibition and neurosurgical cerebrospinal fluid diversion when needed
Reassure and observe idiopathic folds in hyperopic patients, providing refractive correction for the hyperopic error
Exclude a retrobulbar mass or posterior scleritis with orbital and brain imaging in new-onset unilateral folds, especially with proptosis or disc swelling
Monitor visual acuity, refraction and fold morphology with optical coherence tomography over time
Coordinate care across ophthalmology, neurology, endocrinology and orbital surgery according to the underlying cause
